metadata.title: Identifying emergent roles and their relationship with learning outcomes and collaborative problem-solving skills

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study used a small, convenience sample of 54 undergraduates and postgraduates from a normal university in Beijing who participated in a 3-hour collaborative problem-solving (CPS) task. The paper does not report any complex survey design, sampling weights, or replicate-weight procedures, and the analysis is based on questionnaire measures and coded discourse/mind-map outcomes rather than an ILSA-style representative sampling frame. Because no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or stratification/cluster design is described, weighting should not be applied when reproducing the analysis. For any future scaling to large-scale assessments, the authors’ approach would need explicit documentation of sampling weights and PV/scaling procedures if achievement scores were used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values (PVs). The dependent variables are learning outcomes scored from mind maps and CPS skills coded from discourse, which are not PV-based constructs generated by OECD/IEA scaling procedures. Missing-data handling is therefore not documented for PVs; additionally, the manuscript does not describe any missingness-imputation or exclusion rules for questionnaire or coded outcomes, which is a reporting gap for reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 54 undergraduates and postgraduates from a normal university in Beijing. They completed a pre-test questionnaire measuring achievement motivation and self-reported statistics knowledge, were then assigned into 18 heterogeneous triads based on questionnaire responses, and participated in a 120-minute CPS activity plus pre- and post-30-minute mind-map tasks. The analysis uses the full set of participants who completed the pre-test, CPS activity, and both mind-map assessments; the paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the triad assignment procedure.

main_findings.dataset_used: CPS experiment (Beijing university) — emergent roles coding and mind-map learning outcomes
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical regression: Model 1 adjusted R2 = 0.066 (R2 = 6.6%); Model 2 adjusted R2 = 0.210 (R2 = 21.0%), Model 2 p < 0.05. Coefficients (Model 2): Prior knowledge B = 0.078, p = 0.627; Achievement motivation B = 0.213, p = 0.179; Knowledge seeker B = -0.443, p = 0.035; Distractor B = -0.472, p = 0.029; Harmonizer B = 0.332, p = 0.057. Correlations: Prior knowledge with LO r = 0.279*; Harmonizer with LO r = -0.359** (as reported in Table 5 matrix).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the CPS experiment data (coded emergent roles and mind-map learning outcomes), the study leveraged prior knowledge, achievement motivation, knowledge seeker role, distractor role, and harmonizer role to predict learning outcomes, finding that adding emergent roles increased explained variance from 6.6% to 21.0% and that knowledge seekers and distractors were associated with lower learning outcomes (p < 0.05), while harmonizers showed marginal positive association (p = 0.057). This indicates that designing CPS supports to reduce distractive participation and to foster socio-emotional harmonizing may improve learning outcomes, though the study is correlational and based on a small, non-representative sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: CPS experiment (Beijing university) — emergent roles coding and CPS skills ENA
main_findings.target_variable: CPS skills (epistemic network analysis co-occurrence patterns)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ENA results are presented as co-occurrence network patterns (Fig. 4) rather than predictive accuracy metrics; the paper reports qualitative co-occurrence statements (e.g., IG co-occurs with MTF; IS/IG/KP/OP co-occur with negotiation and coordination).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the CPS experiment the study leveraged information giver role, maintaining team function, information seeker role, knowledge provider role, and opinion provider role to characterize CPS skills via epistemic network analysis, finding that information giver co-occurs with maintaining team function and that content- and performance-focused roles co-occur with negotiation and coordination. This indicates that encouraging information sharing and structured negotiation behaviors may strengthen CPS skill development, though the ENA evidence is descriptive (co-occurrence) rather than a causal estimate.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a small CPS experiment with 54 undergraduates and postgraduates from a Beijing normal university (China). Participants completed pre-questionnaires on achievement motivation and self-reported statistics knowledge, were assigned into 18 heterogeneous triads, and then completed a 120-minute CPS task (“migration of workers”) with pre/post mind maps scored by trained coders and turn-level coding of emergent roles. For learning outcomes, hierarchical regression showed Model 1 explained 6.6% of variance (adjusted R2 = 0.066) and Model 2 increased to 21.0% (adjusted R2 = 0.210), with knowledge seeker and distractor roles significantly predicting lower learning outcomes (p = 0.035 and p = 0.029). For CPS skills, epistemic network analysis reported co-occurrence patterns (e.g., information giver with maintaining team function; IS/IG/KP/OP with negotiation and coordination) without predictive metrics. Limitations include non-representative sampling, no survey-weighting, and no documented missing-data strategy.
